clue.text: Staple food in second and last course reduced

parts.note: the last course of a meal is the pudding, cut short to the informal pud

explanation.surface: A menu note: something basic served between a second helping and a shortened dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: PUD is British slang for pudding, i.e. dessert, the last course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Spud is informal for potato, the staple food of Ireland in this St Patrick's Day puzzle.

clue.text: Boy present for a musical performance

parts.note: a boy is a son
to be present is to be at a place

explanation.surface: A lad is in attendance for a recital.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a musical composition, here one being performed for an audience.

clue.text: Remained dormant in Ireland after one's left with Edward

indicators.note: one's left means the I has gone away from the word before it

parts.note: Hibernia is the Latin name for Ireland
one is the Roman numeral I
Ted is a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: Someone stayed inactive in Ireland once a companion departed, keeping only Edward for company.
explanation.walkthrough: Hibernia is the Roman name for Ireland, so the clue's 'Ireland' gives a Latin word; 'left' means departed, not the political side.
explanation.definitionFit: To hibernate is to pass the winter inactive, so having hibernated is having stayed asleep or torpid.

clue.text: Indication of agreement a company set up for playwright

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means the words are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: saying yes indicates agreement

explanation.surface: A nod of approval leads a firm to stage a dramatist's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns YESACO round to give OCASEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sean O'Casey was the Irish dramatist who wrote Juno and the Paycock.

clue.text: 18, for example, I malign

parts.note: to malign someone is to slander them

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to badmouthing a particular person.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is IRISHMAN; an Irishman lives on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irishman is an example of an inhabitant of an island, Ireland.

clue.text: Cheer up with piano that's traditionally played in Ireland

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: rah is a cheer
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Raise morale with a piano tune, as is done in Irish tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' means read from the bottom; 'piano' is the musical marking, not the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The harp is the traditional Irish instrument and a national emblem of Ireland.

clue.text: Teenager's drunk nonalcoholic drink suitable for today?

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters reeling into a new order

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter, so the fodder is just the word for an adolescent

explanation.surface: An adolescent has knocked back a soft drink fitting for the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of TEENAGER gives the answer. Today is St Patrick's Day, when everything is green.
explanation.definitionFit: Green tea is an unfermented tea, a soft drink whose colour suits St Patrick's Day.

clue.text: Irish tax that's somewhat excessive

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the next word is used

explanation.surface: An Irish levy that is a bit over the top.
explanation.definitionFit: A cess was a tax or levy, especially in Ireland, historically for supplying soldiers.

clue.text: Old verse penned by some rulers in parts of Ireland

indicators.note: penned by means held inside, as in an enclosure

parts.note: princes are some rulers

explanation.surface: Ancient poetry written by several monarchs in regions of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penned' looks like writing, but it means enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland has four historic provinces: Ulster, Munster, Leinster and Connacht.

clue.text: Bird's nest found in country area put back

indicators.note: put back means the letters run in reverse order

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A bird's home discovered in rural land was replaced.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerie (eyrie) is the high nest of an eagle or other bird of prey.

clue.text: Duke, libertine, sailor, MP and knight

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute man, a libertine

explanation.surface: A list of a man's roles: aristocrat, womaniser, seaman, politician and knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake was an Elizabethan seafarer, a Member of Parliament and was knighted.

clue.text: Rascals taking naps sleep badly

indicators.note: badly signals the letters are put together wrongly

explanation.surface: Scoundrels who doze in the day then have restless nights.
explanation.definitionFit: Spalpeen is an Irish word for a scamp or good-for-nothing.

clue.text: Left thrown in fight — Paddy's harmless nonsense

indicators.note: thrown in means put inside the other word

parts.note: a barney is British slang for a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A political left gets mixed into a scrap, producing Irish blather.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy is a nickname for an Irishman; the Blarney Stone in County Cork is said to give the gift of the gab.
explanation.definitionFit: Blarney is flattering, smooth talk, the charming nonsense associated with the Irish.

clue.text: Attached to foundation since being retired?

indicators.note: being here means existing within, so the word for since sits inside the bed

parts.note: someone retired for the night is in bed
as can mean since, as in 'as it rained'

explanation.surface: Wondering whether someone is tied to an institution because they have stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' suggests stopping work, but it means having gone to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something based is grounded or founded on something, tied to its foundation.

clue.text: Appointed as agent, as expressed in legal document

indicators.note: in means one word is placed within the other

parts.note: a deed is a signed legal document
a thing expressed is put in words

explanation.surface: Someone was made a representative, as a contract states.
explanation.definitionFit: To depute someone is to delegate them to act on your behalf.

clue.text: Piece of 1 in container — cooked it with a chop

parts.note: a pot is a container

indicators.note: cooked means the letters are prepared in a new way

explanation.surface: A recipe: put it in a pan and fry it with a cutlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 is SPUD, a potato.
explanation.definitionFit: A potato chip is a slice of potato, a crisp or fry made from the spud.

clue.text: Row after daughter had a Guinness, say

indicators.note: after places the row behind the daughter in the answer

parts.note: a rank is a row of soldiers

explanation.surface: An argument once the girl had a stout.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinness is an Irish stout, so having one is an example of having taken a drink.

clue.text: Legendary snake handler, in past, contrived a deception

indicators.note: contrived means artfully rearranged

parts.note: a trick is a deception

explanation.surface: A mythical serpent wrangler once pulled off a con.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrived' rearranges IN PAST into SAINTP.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says Ireland's patron saint drove all the snakes out of the country.

clue.text: For instance, Shaw creating non-U flower person

parts.note: the iris is a flower

indicators.note: non-U means without the letter U, punning on the term for not upper class

parts.note: a human is a person

explanation.surface: George Bernard Shaw writing about an unrefined gardener.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang for not upper-class; here it says drop U from HUMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw was born in Dublin, so he is one example of a man from Ireland.

clue.text: So-called teacher of Irish trimmed back

indicators.note: back means the remaining letters are read in reverse
trimmed means the word loses its outside letters

explanation.surface: An Irish schoolmaster in the habit of being cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trimmed' takes I and H off, leaving RIS; 'back' turns it to SIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Schoolchildren address a male teacher as sir, so the title is what he is called.

clue.text: Irish pubs feeling incomplete without barmaid

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, surrounding
incomplete means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a sense is a feeling
Hebe was the cupbearer of the Greek gods, a crossword barmaid

explanation.surface: Bars in Ireland seeming not quite right with no one serving drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like lacking but means outside: SENS wraps HEBE.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed drinking house in Ireland.

clue.text: Piece of jewellery one found in ancient site near Dublin

indicators.note: found in means placed inside

parts.note: the Hill of Tara in County Meath was the seat of Ireland's high kings
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An item of jewellery unearthed at an archaeological site near Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental headband.

clue.text: Queen preserved, in a way — turned into mythological heroine

indicators.note: turned means the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
drying is one method of preserving food

explanation.surface: A monarch embalmed somehow becomes a figure of myth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses ERDRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Deirdre of the Sorrows is the tragic heroine of Irish legend.

clue.text: See 17
Illicit stuff has power over young person

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over
a teen is a young person

explanation.surface: Banned substances give someone control of a youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: Poteen is Irish moonshine, an illegally distilled spirit.

clue.text: Statement Dorian Gray didn't make put in picture

definitions.meaning: Wilde's Dorian Gray never grew old

explanation.surface: A remark the unageing Wilde character never uttered, rendered in a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oscar Wilde's novel the portrait ages while Dorian stays young.
explanation.definitionFit: Imaged means depicted or represented visually, put into a picture.

clue.text: Emerging forcefully from hot Irish capital in fall

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the fall

parts.note: a descent is a fall

indicators.note: capital means the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Bursting out of a heated Irish city during autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall' sounds like autumn but means descent.
explanation.definitionFit: Dehiscent describes seed pods that split open to release their contents.

clue.text: Guardian, for example, hasn't finished making house in Ireland

indicators.note: hasn't finished means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: The Guardian is a daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper's incomplete coverage of an Irish building project.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dail is the lower chamber of the Irish parliament.

clue.text: Traditional Irish dish in Wild West

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters run riot

explanation.surface: An Irish meal served on the American frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild West' reads as one phrase; Wild is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish stew of mutton, potatoes and onions is the classic Irish dish.

clue.text: Limerick's next for this English poet

definitions.meaning: John ... was the Northamptonshire peasant poet

explanation.surface: The neighbouring county supplies the name of a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Limerick looks like the verse form but is the Irish county.
explanation.definitionFit: John Clare was a nineteenth-century English rural poet; Clare is also an Irish county.

clue.text: Conversed in old language? Just the opposite

indicators.note: in, read the opposite way round, says the old language lies within the other word
the reverse of what is stated: the language is in the word, not the word in the language

explanation.surface: Talked in an archaic tongue, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the clue gives 'old language in Conversed', so the answer sits inside cONVERSEd.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language of Ireland and Scotland.

clue.text: Incensed as Irish scoffed

parts.note: to scoff food is to eat it greedily

explanation.surface: Angry, like the Irish who wolfed their dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate means angry; incensed means enraged.

clue.text: Poverty observed, going west — has food taken in

indicators.note: taken in means placed inside
going west in an across clue means reading right to left

parts.note: observed means seen
dines means has food

explanation.surface: Destitution noticed by a traveller heading west who gets fed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going west' turns SEEN into NEES, which takes in DINES.
explanation.definitionFit: Neediness is the state of lacking necessities, a synonym of poverty.
